en.title: Accounting at university and college
en.short: What an accounting degree, HND or professional foundation covers, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These summaries are for learning. They are not professional, tax or legal advice. Standards, tax rates and laws change, and they differ between countries. Before you rely on a rule, check the current official source. That means the IFRS Foundation, the IAASB, your tax authority or your professional body.

This course assumes you know double entry, the trial balance and basic final accounts. Those are in the school course. Here the questions become harder: how to measure a transaction, which standard applies, and who can rely on the numbers.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Accounting identifies, measures and reports economic information so that people can make decisions. Financial accounting serves people outside the business, such as investors and lenders. Management accounting serves people inside it. Auditing gives an independent opinion on reported information. Taxation works out what is owed to the state under the law. Corporate finance decides how to raise money and where to invest it.

Good accounting is a matter of judgement as well as arithmetic. Two trained accountants can reach different estimates of a provision or an asset’s useful life. Standards limit that freedom, and ethics governs how it is used.

sections.heading: How study is usually organised
sections.text:
A BSc in Accounting usually lasts three to five years, depending on the country. In Nigeria, the NUC benchmarks guide university degrees and the NBTE guides the ND and HND. Early years combine accounting with economics, law, statistics and information technology. Later years cover the specialist subjects.

Professional bodies test similar ground. They include ICAN and ANAN in Nigeria, ICAG in Ghana, ICPAK and KASNEB in Kenya, SAICA in South Africa, and ACCA internationally. Some universities have exemptions from certain papers. Check this directly with the body, because the rules change.

A master’s degree goes deeper into advanced reporting and adds research. Students read journal articles and write a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
First come the regulatory framework, company financial statements, inventories and non-current assets, and cash flow statements. Alongside these you study costing, cost behaviour, tax principles, information systems and the law of companies.

The middle years cover the harder standards: revenue, leases, financial instruments, impairment, provisions and deferred tax. Group accounts follow, which many students find the most demanding topic. In the same period you learn budgeting and variance analysis, auditing, ethics, tax computation, investment appraisal, the cost of capital and public sector accounting.

At master’s level you meet advanced reporting issues, forensic accounting and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Accounting is learned by doing. Read an idea once, then attempt a question without looking at the answer. Build every computation in the same layout each time, so that you can find your own errors. Prove your work: a statement of financial position must balance, and a cash flow must reconcile to the movement in cash.

Read standards through the principle first. For each one, ask three questions. When do we recognise the item? At what amount do we measure it? What must we disclose? Use a recent edition, and note which year’s standards and tax laws your exam tests.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often learn the format and miss the reasoning. An examiner wants the reason why a lease creates a liability, as well as the calculation.

Other frequent errors include:
Using an old standard or an old tax rate.
Treating one country’s tax rule as if it applied everywhere.
Calculating goodwill or the non-controlling interest from the wrong date.
Mixing up an auditor’s responsibility with management’s responsibility.
Including sunk costs in a decision, or depreciation in a net present value calculation.
Giving a ratio without explaining what it means for the business.

keyPoints: Financial accounting serves outside users, and management accounting serves inside users.
Most curricula share reporting, costing, audit, tax, finance, law and ethics.
Standards and tax laws change, so always check which edition your exam uses.
Practise full questions and prove that your answers balance.
Tax rules belong to one country, so name the country.

en.title: The regulatory and conceptual framework
en.short: Who sets accounting standards, how countries adopt them, and the concepts behind them.

sections.heading: Who sets the rules
sections.text:
Published accounts need common rules, or users could not compare companies. The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) issues IFRS Accounting Standards. It sits under the IFRS Foundation. Older standards are called IAS and remain in force until they are replaced.

The IASB has no power to make law. Each country decides what to adopt. Nigeria’s Financial Reporting Council, set up under an Act of 2011, oversees reporting, and listed and other significant public interest entities began using IFRS from 2012. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa also use IFRS widely. The UK uses UK-adopted international standards for listed groups and its own FRS 102 for many other companies. The United States uses its own US GAAP, set by the FASB. Smaller entities in many countries may use the simpler IFRS for SMEs.

sections.heading: The Conceptual Framework
sections.text:
The IASB’s Conceptual Framework (revised in 2018) is not a standard, but it guides the writing of standards. It says the main users are investors, lenders and other creditors.

Useful information has two fundamental qualities. It must be relevant, which means it can change a decision, and it must be a faithful representation, which means it is complete, neutral and free from error. Four qualities enhance it: comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability.

sections.heading: Assets and liabilities
sections.text:
An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. A liability is a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Equity is the remainder after deducting liabilities from assets.

Example: Amara’s company plans to buy a machine next year. It has no asset and no liability yet, because no past event has occurred. Once the machine is delivered on credit, the company controls an asset and owes a liability.

keyPoints: The IASB issues IFRS, but each country decides whether to adopt it.
The Conceptual Framework guides standards and does not override them.
Relevance and faithful representation are the two fundamental qualities.
Assets and liabilities both depend on a past event.
Equity is what remains after deducting liabilities from assets.

en.title: Preparing company financial statements
en.short: The full set of financial statements, comprehensive income and changes in equity.

sections.heading: The complete set
sections.text:
A company reporting under IFRS presents a statement of financial position, a statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, a statement of changes in equity, a statement of cash flows, and notes. It also gives comparative figures for the previous period.

IAS 1 has set these presentation rules for many years. IFRS 18, Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements, replaces it for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with earlier use allowed. IFRS 18 sorts income and expenses into five categories: operating, investing, financing, income taxes and discontinued operations. It also requires new subtotals and disclosures about management-defined performance measures. Check which standard your exam uses.

sections.heading: Profit and other comprehensive income
sections.text:
Profit or loss is the main performance measure. Other comprehensive income (OCI) holds certain gains and losses that standards keep outside profit, such as a revaluation gain on property. Total comprehensive income is the sum of both.

Assets and liabilities are split into current and non-current. An item is usually current if it will be realised or settled within twelve months of the reporting date.

sections.heading: Worked example: changes in equity
sections.text:
Bello Ltd starts the year with share capital of ₦5,000,000 and retained earnings of ₦4,000,000. Total equity is ₦9,000,000. During the year its profit is ₦1,500,000, a land revaluation gain is ₦300,000 and dividends paid are ₦600,000.

Total comprehensive income = 1,500,000 + 300,000 = ₦1,800,000.
Closing retained earnings = 4,000,000 + 1,500,000 − 600,000 = ₦4,900,000.
Closing revaluation surplus = ₦300,000.
Closing share capital = ₦5,000,000.
Closing total equity = 5,000,000 + 300,000 + 4,900,000 = ₦10,200,000.

Check: 9,000,000 + 1,800,000 − 600,000 = ₦10,200,000. The two routes agree.

Notice that dividends are not an expense. They are a distribution to owners, so they appear in the statement of changes in equity and not in profit or loss.

keyPoints: A full set has four main statements, plus notes and comparatives.
IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027.
Total comprehensive income is profit or loss plus OCI.
A revaluation gain usually goes to OCI, not to profit.
Dividends reduce equity directly and are not an expense.

en.title: Inventories and property, plant and equipment
en.short: How IAS 2 and IAS 16 measure inventory and long-term assets, including revaluation.

sections.heading: Inventories under IAS 2
sections.text:
Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). Cost includes purchase price, conversion costs and other costs of bringing the goods to their present place and condition. NRV is the expected selling price less the costs to complete and sell. IAS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average where items are interchangeable. It does not allow LIFO.

Example: Zainab holds 500 units that cost ₦1,250 each. Each will sell for ₦1,500, after finishing costs of ₦200 and selling costs of ₦100.
NRV = 1,500 − 200 − 100 = ₦1,200 per unit.
This is below cost, so the write-down = 500 × (1,250 − 1,200) = ₦25,000.

sections.heading: Initial cost under IAS 16
sections.text:
Property, plant and equipment (PPE) is first recorded at cost. Cost includes the purchase price and directly attributable costs of making the asset ready for use. Staff training and general overheads are expensed.

Example: a Ghanaian firm buys a machine for GH₵100,000. It pays GH₵5,000 for delivery, GH₵3,000 for installation, GH₵2,000 for testing and GH₵4,000 for staff training.
Cost = 100,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = GH₵110,000. Training is expensed.

sections.heading: After initial recognition
sections.text:
A company chooses the cost model or the revaluation model for each class of PPE. Under the revaluation model, revaluations must be kept up to date. An increase usually goes to OCI as a revaluation surplus. A decrease goes to profit or loss, unless it reverses an earlier surplus on the same asset.

Example, continued: the machine has a five-year life and a residual value of GH₵10,000.
Annual straight-line depreciation = (110,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = GH₵20,000.
Carrying amount after two years = 110,000 − 40,000 = GH₵70,000.
It is revalued to GH₵85,000, so the surplus = GH₵15,000.
New depreciation = (85,000 − 10,000) ÷ 3 = GH₵25,000 a year.

keyPoints: Inventory is held at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
IAS 2 does not allow LIFO.
PPE cost includes costs of getting the asset ready for use, but not training.
Revaluation gains normally go to OCI as a revaluation surplus.
After revaluation, depreciation is based on the new carrying amount.

en.title: Statement of cash flows
en.short: How IAS 7 reports cash from operating, investing and financing activities.

sections.heading: Why cash flows matter
sections.text:
Profit depends on accruals and estimates. Cash is harder to manipulate and shows whether a business can pay its debts. A profitable firm can still fail if customers pay late.

IAS 7 groups cash flows into three activities. Operating activities are the main revenue-producing activities. Investing activities are purchases and sales of long-term assets. Financing activities change the company’s equity and borrowings. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with little risk of a change in value.

sections.heading: The indirect method
sections.text:
The direct method lists actual receipts and payments. Most companies use the indirect method, which starts from profit and removes non-cash items and working capital movements. Add back depreciation, because it uses no cash. An increase in inventory or receivables reduces cash. An increase in payables keeps cash in the business.

The amendments made with IFRS 18 change some details for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. The indirect method then starts from operating profit, and most companies lose the choice of where to classify interest and dividends.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Figures in pounds for Patel Ltd. The loan interest expense was paid in full. PPE was sold at its carrying amount.

Profit before tax 60,000
Add depreciation 15,000
Add interest expense 5,000
Increase in inventories (4,000)
Increase in receivables (6,000)
Increase in payables 3,000
Cash generated from operations 73,000
Interest paid (5,000)
Tax paid (12,000)
Net cash from operating activities 56,000

Purchase of PPE (30,000)
Proceeds from sale of PPE 8,000
Net cash used in investing activities (22,000)

Shares issued 10,000
Loan repaid (20,000)
Dividends paid (9,000)
Net cash used in financing activities (19,000)

Net increase in cash = 56,000 − 22,000 − 19,000 = 15,000.
Opening cash 7,000 + 15,000 = closing cash 22,000.

The closing figure must agree with the statement of financial position.

keyPoints: IAS 7 uses three headings: operating, investing and financing.
Depreciation is added back because it is not a cash flow.
An increase in receivables or inventory reduces operating cash.
An increase in payables increases operating cash.
The net movement must reconcile opening cash to closing cash.

en.title: Cost concepts and absorption costing
en.short: Classifying costs, charging overheads to products and finding under or over absorption.

sections.heading: Classifying costs
sections.text:
Cost accounting tells managers what things cost. Costs can be classified in several ways, depending on the purpose.

By traceability: a direct cost can be traced to one product, such as its raw material. An indirect cost, or overhead, is shared, such as factory rent.
By behaviour: a variable cost changes in total with output, and a fixed cost stays the same within a relevant range. A semi-variable cost has both parts.
By function: production, selling, distribution and administration.

Costing systems depend on the work. Job costing suits custom orders. Batch costing suits groups of identical items. Process costing suits continuous production, such as cement or flour.

sections.heading: Absorbing overheads
sections.text:
Absorption costing charges a share of production overheads to each unit. There are three steps. Allocate costs that belong wholly to one cost centre. Apportion shared costs on a fair basis, such as floor area for rent. Then absorb each production department’s overhead into units, using a predetermined rate.

Rate = budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity.

Service department costs are reapportioned to production departments first, because products do not pass through them.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
The machining department of a Lagos factory budgets overheads of ₦2,400,000 and 80,000 machine hours.
Rate = 2,400,000 ÷ 80,000 = ₦30 per machine hour.

Job 17 uses materials of ₦40,000, direct labour of ₦25,000 and 200 machine hours.
Job cost = 40,000 + 25,000 + (200 × 30) = ₦71,000.

Actual overheads turn out to be ₦2,500,000 and actual machine hours are 85,000.
Absorbed = 85,000 × 30 = ₦2,550,000.
Over absorption = 2,550,000 − 2,500,000 = ₦50,000.

More overhead was charged to production than was actually incurred. So ₦50,000 is credited to profit or loss at the period end. Under absorption would be an extra charge.

Activity-based costing refines this idea. It uses several cost drivers, such as the number of set-ups, in place of a single rate.

keyPoints: A direct cost can be traced to one product, and an overhead is shared.
The overhead rate is budgeted overhead divided by budgeted activity.
Absorbed overhead is actual activity multiplied by the predetermined rate.
Over absorption adds to profit, and under absorption reduces it.
Activity-based costing uses several cost drivers.

en.title: Marginal costing, CVP and short-term decisions
en.short: Contribution, break-even analysis, margin of safety and relevant costs for decisions.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text:
Marginal costing treats only variable costs as product costs. Fixed costs are charged in full against the period’s contribution.

Contribution = sales − variable costs.

Contribution first covers fixed costs, and then it creates profit. Reported profit can differ from absorption costing when inventory levels change. This is because absorption costing carries some fixed overhead forward in closing inventory.

sections.heading: Worked example: CVP
sections.text:
Cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis studies how profit changes with output. A Nairobi firm sells a product for KSh 1,000. The variable cost is KSh 600, and fixed costs are KSh 2,000,000 a year.

Contribution per unit = 1,000 − 600 = KSh 400.
Contribution to sales ratio = 400 ÷ 1,000 = 40%.
Break-even = 2,000,000 ÷ 400 = 5,000 units, or KSh 5,000,000 of sales.
Units for a profit of KSh 600,000 = 2,600,000 ÷ 400 = 6,500 units.
If budgeted sales are 7,000 units, the margin of safety = 7,000 − 5,000 = 2,000 units. That is 2,000 ÷ 7,000 = 28.6% of budget.

CVP assumes that prices and unit variable costs stay constant and that fixed costs do not change. These assumptions hold only within a limited range.

sections.heading: Relevant costs
sections.text:
A decision should use relevant costs, which are future, incremental cash flows that differ between the options. A sunk cost has already been spent and is ignored. Committed costs and apportioned overheads that do not change are ignored too. An opportunity cost, the benefit lost from the next best option, is included.

Example: a customer offers KSh 750 a unit for a one-off order of 1,000 units. The firm has spare capacity, and fixed costs will not change.
Extra contribution = 1,000 × (750 − 600) = KSh 150,000.
On these figures the order adds profit, although its price is below the full cost per unit. Managers should still consider whether regular customers might demand the lower price.

keyPoints: Contribution equals sales minus variable costs.
Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.
Margin of safety is budgeted sales minus break-even sales.
Sunk costs are never relevant to a decision.
Marginal and absorption profit differ when inventory levels change.

en.title: Principles of taxation
en.short: What tax is for, the canons of a good tax, direct and indirect taxes, and how VAT works.

sections.heading: What taxes do
sections.text:
A tax is a compulsory payment to government, with no direct benefit promised in return. Taxes raise revenue, redistribute income and influence behaviour. They can also protect local industries or discourage harmful goods.

Adam Smith set out four canons of a good tax in 1776. These are equity, certainty, convenience and economy. Modern writers add efficiency, neutrality and simplicity.

Tax law belongs to each country. Rates, reliefs and definitions differ, and they change often. Check the current law before relying on any rule.

sections.heading: Types of tax
sections.text:
A direct tax is paid by the person it is imposed on, such as tax on income. An indirect tax is collected through someone else, usually a seller, and is passed on in the price, such as value added tax (VAT). Tax incidence asks who finally bears the burden.

A progressive tax takes a higher percentage as income rises. A proportional tax takes the same percentage from everyone. A regressive tax takes a larger share of a low income than of a high one. A flat tax on goods can be regressive, because poorer households spend more of their income.

Tax avoidance uses the law to reduce tax, although anti-avoidance rules can cancel the benefit. Tax evasion is deliberately hiding income or giving false information, and it is a crime.

sections.heading: How VAT works
sections.text:
A VAT-registered business charges output VAT on sales and recovers input VAT on allowed purchases. It pays the difference to the tax authority. The final consumer bears the cost.

Example in Nigeria, where the standard rate is 7.5%. Bisi’s firm sells goods for ₦2,000,000 and buys taxable inputs for ₦1,200,000, both before VAT.
Output VAT = 2,000,000 × 7.5% = ₦150,000.
Input VAT = 1,200,000 × 7.5% = ₦90,000.
VAT payable = 150,000 − 90,000 = ₦60,000.

Rates differ elsewhere. The UK standard rate is 20%. Ghana’s structure combines VAT with two levies, and it was revised by a new VAT Act from 2026.

keyPoints: Smith’s four canons are equity, certainty, convenience and economy.
A progressive tax takes a higher percentage as income rises.
Avoidance uses the law, and evasion breaks it.
VAT payable is output VAT minus allowed input VAT.
Tax law is national, and it changes often.

en.title: Accounting information systems
en.short: How transactions become reports, the controls that protect data and the use of ERP systems.

sections.heading: From transaction to report
sections.text:
An accounting information system (AIS) collects, stores and processes financial data, and turns it into reports. It combines people, procedures, data, software and hardware.

Transactions are often grouped into cycles. The revenue cycle runs from a customer’s order to the receipt of cash. The expenditure cycle runs from a purchase request to the payment of a supplier. There are also payroll, production and financial reporting cycles. An enterprise resource planning (ERP) system links these in one shared database. A sale can then update inventory, receivables and the ledger at once. A small business might use cloud accounting software for similar results.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.text:
Internal controls protect assets and data. General controls apply to the whole IT environment. Examples are user passwords, access rights, back-ups, change management and physical security. Application controls apply to one process. Examples are validation checks, sequence checks and batch totals.

Segregation of duties means that one person should not authorise a transaction, record it and hold the related asset. In a small business this may be hard, so owner review becomes important.

Example: three supplier invoices of 1,200, 3,450 and 780 are entered as a batch. The control total is 5,430. If the system total differs, someone investigates before posting.

A three-way match compares the purchase order, the goods received note and the supplier’s invoice before payment.

sections.heading: Data, law and new tools
sections.text:
An audit trail lets a reviewer follow a transaction from its source to the reports and back. Data analytics can test whole populations of transactions, for example to look for duplicate payments.

Data protection laws apply to customer and staff information. Examples are Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023, Ghana’s Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) and the UK GDPR. Tax authorities are also moving to electronic invoicing, including in Nigeria and Ghana. Check the current requirements for your country.

keyPoints: An ERP system links business cycles in one shared database.
General controls cover the IT environment, and application controls cover one process.
Segregation of duties separates authorising, recording and custody.
A three-way match compares order, goods received note and invoice.
An audit trail links a report back to its source documents.

en.title: Company law for accountants: forming a company
en.short: Corporate personality, types of company, company formation and the main company statutes.

sections.heading: Corporate personality
sections.text:
A registered company is a legal person, separate from its members. It can own property, make contracts, sue and be sued. The UK case Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd (1897) established the principle, and common law systems follow it. Courts may look behind the company, called lifting the veil, in limited cases such as fraud.

Limited liability means that members can lose only what they have paid or agreed to pay for their shares.

sections.heading: Statutes and types of company
sections.text:
Company statutes differ between countries. Nigeria has the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (CAMA), administered by the Corporate Affairs Commission. Ghana has the Companies Act 2019 (Act 992), which replaced the 1963 Act. The UK has the Companies Act 2006.

Companies may be limited by shares, limited by guarantee or unlimited. A public company can offer shares to the public. A private company cannot. CAMA 2020 allows a private company to have one member. It also exempts certain small companies from audit.

The CAMA small company test uses a turnover of not more than ₦120 million and net assets of not more than ₦60 million, with other conditions. This is not the same as the small company test for tax.

sections.heading: Formation and the constitution
sections.text:
To form a company, promoters file documents with the registrar. Registration brings the company into being. A promoter who signs a contract before that date may be personally liable, unless the law or the contract provides otherwise.

The constitution sets out the company’s internal rules. It is commonly called the memorandum and articles of association, although terms vary by country. It is a contract between the company and its members.

Example: Ngozi and Tunde invest ₦500,000 each in a new company, which later fails with debts of ₦5,000,000. If their shares are fully paid and they gave no guarantees, they lose their ₦1,000,000 of investment. Creditors bear the rest of the loss.

keyPoints: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members.
Salomon (UK, 1897) is the classic authority on separate personality.
CAMA 2020 governs Nigerian companies, and Act 992 governs Ghanaian companies.
Limited liability caps a member’s loss at the amount due on the shares.
The company law and tax definitions of a small company are different tests.

en.title: Interpreting financial statements
en.short: Profitability, gearing and earnings per share, and how to explain what they mean.

sections.heading: From calculation to explanation
sections.text:
Ratios only raise questions. An analyst compares them with earlier years, with competitors and with the industry. The analyst then looks for causes in the notes and in the business itself. A falling margin might result from price cuts, higher input costs or a change in sales mix.

Limits matter too. Accounts are historical, companies use different accounting policies, and year-end figures may not be typical. In high inflation, assets held at old costs can make returns look better than they are.

sections.heading: Worked example: performance and risk
sections.text:
Figures in rand for Mokoena Ltd:
Revenue 800,000
Profit before interest and tax 96,000
Interest 16,000
Tax 20,000
Profit for the year 60,000
Equity 400,000
Long-term debt 200,000

Capital employed = 400,000 + 200,000 = R600,000.
Return on capital employed (ROCE) = 96,000 ÷ 600,000 = 16%.
Operating margin = 96,000 ÷ 800,000 = 12%.
Asset turnover = 800,000 ÷ 600,000 = 1.33 times.
Check: 12% × 1.33 = 16%.
Gearing = 200,000 ÷ 600,000 = 33.3%.
Interest cover = 96,000 ÷ 16,000 = 6 times.

ROCE splits into margin and turnover. So the firm can raise its return either by earning more on each sale or by using its assets more fully.

sections.heading: Earnings per share
sections.text:
IAS 33 requires listed entities to report earnings per share (EPS). Basic EPS is profit attributable to ordinary shareholders, divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares in issue.

Mokoena has 100,000 shares on 1 January. It issues 30,000 more at full market price on 1 October, and its year ends on 31 December.
Weighted average = 100,000 + (30,000 × 3 ÷ 12) = 107,500 shares.
Basic EPS = R60,000 ÷ 107,500 = R0.56, to two decimal places.

Diluted EPS shows the effect if convertible instruments or share options became ordinary shares. It warns investors about possible future dilution.

keyPoints: ROCE equals operating margin multiplied by asset turnover.
Gearing here is debt divided by debt plus equity, but definitions vary.
Interest cover shows how easily profit covers interest.
Basic EPS uses the weighted average number of shares.
Always explain the cause of a ratio change.

en.title: Revenue from contracts with customers
en.short: The five-step model in IFRS 15, with a worked contract allocating a bundled price.

sections.heading: The five steps
sections.text:
IFRS 15 has one principle. An entity recognises revenue to show the transfer of promised goods or services to customers, at the amount it expects to be entitled to. It applies five steps:

1. Identify the contract with the customer.
2. Identify the performance obligations, which are the distinct promises.
3. Determine the transaction price.
4. Allocate the price to the obligations, based on stand-alone selling prices.
5. Recognise revenue when, or as, each obligation is satisfied.

Revenue is recognised over time if certain conditions are met, for example if the customer receives the benefit as the entity performs. Otherwise it is recognised at a point in time, when the customer obtains control. Variable amounts, such as bonuses and expected returns, are estimated and included only as far as a significant reversal is highly unlikely.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
On 1 October, a Nigerian software firm signs a contract for ₦1,200,000, paid in advance. It promises a software licence, installation and twelve months of support. The three are distinct, and the licence is a right to use the software as delivered. Stand-alone prices are ₦900,000, ₦150,000 and ₦450,000, which total ₦1,500,000.

Allocation ratio = 1,200,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 0.8.
Licence: 900,000 × 0.8 = ₦720,000.
Installation: 150,000 × 0.8 = ₦120,000.
Support: 450,000 × 0.8 = ₦360,000.
Total: ₦1,200,000.

The licence and installation are delivered in October. Support is earned evenly at ₦30,000 a month.

Revenue to 31 December = 720,000 + 120,000 + (3 × 30,000) = ₦930,000.
Contract liability = 1,200,000 − 930,000 = ₦270,000, which is nine months of support.

sections.heading: Judgement and disclosure
sections.text:
A contract liability arises when the customer has paid before the entity performs. A contract asset arises when the entity has performed but its right to payment depends on something other than time.

Common judgements include whether promises are distinct, and whether an entity is a principal or an agent. An agent reports only its commission as revenue.

keyPoints: IFRS 15 uses a five-step model for all customer contracts, with some exclusions.
A bundled price is allocated by relative stand-alone selling prices.
Revenue is recognised when control passes to the customer.
Cash received before performance is a contract liability.
An agent recognises only its commission.

en.title: Intangibles, impairment and provisions
en.short: IAS 38, IAS 36 and IAS 37: development costs, recoverable amount, provisions and contingencies.

sections.heading: Intangible assets
sections.text: IAS 38 covers identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, such as licences. Research costs are expensed. Development costs must be capitalised once the entity can show six things: technical feasibility, the intention to complete, the ability to use or sell, probable future benefits, adequate resources, and reliable measurement of the cost. Internally generated brands and goodwill are not recognised as assets.

sections.heading: Impairment
sections.text:
IAS 36 ensures that assets are not carried above what can be recovered. Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Value in use is the present value of future cash flows from the asset. An impairment loss is the carrying amount minus the recoverable amount.

Example: a machine in Accra has a carrying amount of GH₵500,000. Its fair value less costs of disposal is GH₵420,000, and its value in use is GH₵460,000.
Recoverable amount = GH₵460,000.
Impairment loss = 500,000 − 460,000 = GH₵40,000.

Goodwill is tested every year, and an impairment of goodwill cannot be reversed.

sections.heading: Provisions and contingencies
sections.text:
IAS 37 requires a provision when three conditions are met. There is a present obligation from a past event. An outflow is probable. A reliable estimate can be made. A future operating loss does not qualify.

Example: a Kenyan firm sold 500 items under warranty in its last month. It expects no claim on 70%, a minor repair of KSh 10,000 on 20%, and a major repair of KSh 60,000 on 10%.
Expected cost per item = (0.2 × 10,000) + (0.1 × 60,000) = KSh 8,000.
Provision = 500 × 8,000 = KSh 4,000,000.

A contingent liability is disclosed, not recognised, unless an outflow is remote. A contingent asset is disclosed only when an inflow is probable.

IAS 10 deals with events after the reporting period. Events that show conditions existing at the reporting date adjust the accounts. Other events, if material, are only disclosed.

keyPoints: Research is expensed, and qualifying development is capitalised.
Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.
Goodwill impairment is never reversed.
A provision needs an obligation, a probable outflow and a reliable estimate.
Contingent liabilities are disclosed and contingent assets are not recognised.

en.title: Leases
en.short: How lessees and lessors account for leases under IFRS 16, with a worked lease liability.

sections.heading: What IFRS 16 changed
sections.text:
A lease gives the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period, in return for payment. IFRS 16 replaced IAS 17 and applies to annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2019.

For lessees, almost all leases now appear on the statement of financial position. The lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. There are two optional exemptions: short-term leases of twelve months or less, and leases of low-value assets.

Lessors still classify a lease as a finance lease or an operating lease. A finance lease transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership.

sections.heading: Measurement by the lessee
sections.text: The lease liability starts as the present value of the lease payments not yet paid, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or, if that is unknown, at the lessee’s incremental borrowing rate. The right-of-use asset equals this liability, plus initial direct costs, payments made at or before the start (less incentives received) and any estimated restoration costs. The asset is normally depreciated, and the liability grows by interest and falls by payments.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Sarah’s company in the UK leases equipment for three years. It pays £10,000 at the end of each year, and the discount rate is 5%.

Present value = 10,000 ÷ 1.05 + 10,000 ÷ 1.05² + 10,000 ÷ 1.05³ = £27,232.

Year 1: 27,232 + interest 1,362 − payment 10,000 = 18,594.
Year 2: 18,594 + interest 930 − payment 10,000 = 9,524.
Year 3: 9,524 + interest 476 − payment 10,000 = 0.

Total interest = 1,362 + 930 + 476 = £2,768, which equals 30,000 − 27,232.

Right-of-use depreciation = 27,232 ÷ 3 = £9,077 a year.

Year 1 expense in profit or loss = 1,362 + 9,077 = £10,439. This is more than the £10,000 paid, because interest is highest at the start.

keyPoints: Lessees put almost all leases on the statement of financial position.
The liability starts at the present value of the unpaid lease payments.
Short-term and low-value leases can be exempt.
Lessors still separate finance and operating leases.
Expense is higher early in the lease because interest falls over time.

en.title: Financial instruments
en.short: Classifying debt and equity, measuring financial assets under IFRS 9 and the effective interest method.

sections.heading: Debt or equity
sections.text: A financial instrument creates a financial asset for one party and a financial liability or equity for the other. IAS 32 looks at substance. If the issuer has a contractual obligation to deliver cash, the instrument is a liability, even if it is called a share. Redeemable preference shares are often liabilities. A convertible bond is split into a liability part and an equity part.

sections.heading: Classifying financial assets
sections.text:
IFRS 9 uses two tests for debt instruments held as assets: the business model and the cash flow characteristics.

Amortised cost applies if the entity holds the asset to collect contractual cash flows, and those flows are solely payments of principal and interest.
Fair value through OCI (FVOCI) applies if the entity holds to collect and also to sell.
Fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL) is used for everything else.

Equity investments normally go to FVTPL. An entity may choose, on first recognition, to use FVOCI for equity not held for trading.

IFRS 9 also uses expected credit losses. Allowances are based on expected losses, so a loss event need not have happened yet. For many assets the allowance starts at twelve-month losses and moves to lifetime losses when credit risk rises significantly.

sections.heading: Worked example: effective interest
sections.text:
A Kenyan company issues a three-year loan note with a nominal value of KSh 1,000,000 for KSh 950,000. It pays interest of 6% on the nominal value each year end and repays at par. The effective rate is about 7.94%. This is the rate that discounts the future payments to KSh 950,000.

Year 1: 950,000 + 75,411 − 60,000 = 965,411.
Year 2: 965,411 + 76,634 − 60,000 = 982,045.
Year 3: 982,045 + 77,955 − 60,000 = 1,000,000.

The finance cost in profit or loss is the effective interest, not the cash paid. Total finance cost = 75,411 + 76,634 + 77,955 = KSh 230,000. This equals the cash interest of 180,000 plus the discount of 50,000.

keyPoints: IAS 32 classifies by substance, not legal name.
IFRS 9 tests the business model and the cash flow characteristics.
The three categories are amortised cost, FVOCI and FVTPL.
The finance cost uses the effective interest rate.
IFRS 9 uses an expected credit loss model.

en.title: Income taxes and deferred tax
en.short: Current and deferred tax under IAS 12, with a worked temporary difference.

sections.heading: Two parts of the tax charge
sections.text:
IAS 12 divides the tax charge into current tax and deferred tax. Current tax is the amount payable on the taxable profit for the period. Taxable profit often differs from accounting profit.

Some differences are permanent. A fine that the tax law does not allow as a deduction never affects taxable profit in any year. Others are temporary. An item may be deductible for tax earlier or later than it is expensed in the accounts.

Deferred tax accounts for the future tax effect of temporary differences. IAS 12 looks at the statement of financial position. A temporary difference is the carrying amount of an asset or liability minus its tax base. The tax base is the amount attributed to that item for tax purposes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A South African company has profit before tax of R500,000, after depreciation of R20,000. Tax depreciation for the year is R40,000. The asset cost R100,000 at the start of the year. The tax rate is 27%, South Africa’s company rate at the time of writing.

Taxable profit = 500,000 + 20,000 − 40,000 = R480,000.
Current tax = 480,000 × 27% = R129,600.

Carrying amount = 100,000 − 20,000 = R80,000.
Tax base = 100,000 − 40,000 = R60,000.
Taxable temporary difference = 80,000 − 60,000 = R20,000.
Deferred tax liability = 20,000 × 27% = R5,400.

Total tax expense = 129,600 + 5,400 = R135,000.
Check: 500,000 × 27% = R135,000.

The company has paid less tax so far, and it will pay more later. So it records a liability now.

sections.heading: Assets, rates and presentation
sections.text:
A deductible temporary difference can create a deferred tax asset, as can unused tax losses. The asset is recognised only if future taxable profit is probable. Deferred tax is measured at the rates enacted or substantively enacted at the reporting date.

A tax effect follows its item. If a revaluation gain goes to OCI, the related deferred tax also goes to OCI.

keyPoints: Tax expense is current tax plus the movement in deferred tax.
A temporary difference is carrying amount minus tax base.
A permanent difference creates no deferred tax.
Deferred tax assets need probable future taxable profit.
Use the enacted or substantively enacted tax rates.

en.title: Group accounts: consolidated financial position
en.short: When a parent consolidates, and how to calculate goodwill, NCI and group retained earnings.

sections.heading: Control and goodwill
sections.text:
IFRS 10 requires a parent to consolidate its subsidiaries. A parent controls an investee if it has power over the investee, exposure to variable returns from it, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. Owning more than half of the votes usually gives control.

Consolidated accounts add together all the assets and liabilities of parent and subsidiary. The investment in the subsidiary is replaced by goodwill. IFRS 3 measures the subsidiary’s identifiable net assets at fair value on the acquisition date. The non-controlling interest (NCI) is the part not owned by the parent. It may be measured at fair value or at its share of the net assets.

Goodwill = consideration + NCI − fair value of net assets.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Figures in naira. Parent paid 900,000 for 80% of Sub. At acquisition, Sub had share capital of 500,000 and retained earnings of 300,000. Its land was worth 100,000 more than its book value. So fair value of net assets = 900,000. NCI is measured at its share of net assets.

NCI at acquisition = 20% × 900,000 = 180,000.
Goodwill = 900,000 + 180,000 − 900,000 = 180,000.
If NCI had instead been measured at a fair value of 230,000, goodwill would be 230,000.

Today, Sub’s retained earnings are 400,000, a post-acquisition gain of 100,000. Parent has share capital of 2,000,000, retained earnings of 1,000,000 and other net assets of 2,100,000. Goodwill is not impaired.

Group retained earnings = 1,000,000 + (80% × 100,000) = 1,080,000.
NCI = 180,000 + (20% × 100,000) = 200,000.

Net assets: goodwill 180,000 + Parent 2,100,000 + Sub 1,000,000 = 3,280,000.
Equity: 2,000,000 + 1,080,000 + 200,000 = 3,280,000.

Sub’s net assets of 1,000,000 are 500,000 + 400,000 + 100,000. Both totals agree.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Only a subsidiary’s post-acquisition profit enters group retained earnings. Consolidated share capital is the parent’s only. Goodwill is tested for impairment every year.

keyPoints: Consolidation depends on control, not only on the share percentage.
Goodwill equals consideration plus NCI minus fair value of net assets.
NCI can be measured at fair value or at its share of net assets.
Only post-acquisition profits enter group retained earnings.
Consolidated share capital is the parent’s share capital.

en.title: Group accounts: consolidated profit and associates
en.short: Eliminating intra-group trading and unrealised profit, and using the equity method for associates.

sections.heading: Removing intra-group trading
sections.text:
A group reports as one entity, so sales between its members are not real sales. Intra-group sales are removed from both revenue and cost of sales. Intra-group balances are also cancelled.

If goods are still in the group’s inventory at the year end, the seller’s profit on them has not been earned from outsiders. This provision for unrealised profit (PURP) is removed.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Figures in thousands of cedis. Parent owns 80% of Sub. Sub sold goods to Parent for 400, at 25% mark-up on cost. Parent still holds 100 of these goods.

PURP = 100 × 25 ÷ 125 = 20.

Parent: revenue 5,000, cost of sales 3,000, other expenses 800.
Sub: revenue 2,000, cost of sales 1,200, other expenses 400.

Revenue = 5,000 + 2,000 − 400 = 6,600.
Cost of sales = 3,000 + 1,200 − 400 + 20 = 3,820.
Gross profit = 6,600 − 3,820 = 2,780.
Other expenses = 800 + 400 = 1,200.
Group profit = 2,780 − 1,200 = 1,580.

Sub’s own profit = 2,000 − 1,200 − 400 = 400. Sub was the seller, so the NCI shares the adjustment.
NCI share = 20% × (400 − 20) = 76.
Parent’s owners = 1,580 − 76 = 1,504. Tax is ignored.

sections.heading: Associates and joint arrangements
sections.text:
An associate is an entity over which the investor has significant influence, the power to take part in policy decisions. Holding 20% or more of the votes is presumed to give significant influence, unless clearly shown otherwise. IAS 28 requires the equity method, not consolidation.

It starts at cost. It rises by the investor’s share of post-acquisition profit and falls by dividends received.

Example: a company pays 200 for 30% of an associate, which then earns 100 and pays no dividend.
Share of profit = 30% × 100 = 30.
Carrying amount = 200 + 30 = 230.

IFRS 11 covers joint arrangements. A joint venture also uses the equity method.

keyPoints: Intra-group sales are removed from revenue and cost of sales.
PURP is the profit element in intra-group goods still held.
If the subsidiary is the seller, the NCI shares the PURP adjustment.
An associate is shown by the equity method, usually at 20% to 50% holdings.
Associates and joint ventures are not consolidated line by line.

en.title: Budgeting, standard costing and variances
en.short: Types of budget, flexed budgets and how to calculate and explain cost variances.

sections.heading: Budgets
sections.text:
A budget is a plan in money terms for a future period. It helps managers to plan, coordinate, control and motivate. The limiting factor, often sales demand, is budgeted first. Functional budgets then lead to a cash budget and budgeted statements.

An incremental budget adjusts last year’s figures. A zero-based budget makes every cost justify itself from nothing. A rolling budget adds a new period as each one ends. Participation by managers can improve commitment, but it can also lead them to overstate costs, which is called budgetary slack.

A flexed budget restates the budget for the actual output. Comparing actual results with a fixed budget is misleading when output has changed.

sections.heading: Worked example: variances
sections.text:
A UK firm’s standard for one unit is 2 kg of material at £5 per kg, and 3 hours of labour at £8 an hour. It makes 1,000 units.

Material: it buys and uses 2,200 kg at £4.80, costing £10,560.
Standard cost of output = 1,000 × 2 × £5 = £10,000.
Price variance = (5.00 − 4.80) × 2,200 = £440 favourable.
Usage variance = (2,200 − 2,000) × 5 = £1,000 adverse.
Total = £560 adverse, which agrees with 10,560 − 10,000.

Labour: 2,900 hours cost £8.50 an hour, or £24,650.
Standard cost of output = 1,000 × 3 × £8 = £24,000.
Rate variance = (8.50 − 8.00) × 2,900 = £1,450 adverse.
Efficiency variance = (3,000 − 2,900) × 8 = £800 favourable.
Total = £650 adverse, which agrees with 24,650 − 24,000.

sections.heading: Using variances
sections.text:
A variance only points to a question. Cheap material can cause a favourable price variance and an adverse usage variance if it wastes more in production. Better-paid, skilled staff may explain an adverse rate variance and a favourable efficiency variance.

Managers should be judged on what they control. This idea is called responsibility accounting. Many firms also use non-financial measures alongside variances, such as quality and customer service.

keyPoints: A flexed budget restates the plan for actual output.
Price and rate variances use the actual quantity.
Usage and efficiency variances use the standard price or rate.
Sub-variances must add up to the total variance.
Related variances can have one shared cause.

en.title: Auditing: framework, risk and materiality
en.short: What an audit is, the responsibilities it involves, audit risk, materiality and internal control.

sections.heading: What an audit is
sections.text:
An audit gives independent assurance on financial statements. The auditor gives an opinion on whether they show a true and fair view, or are fairly presented, under the applicable framework. ISA 200 describes this overall objective. An audit gives reasonable assurance. This is high, but it is not absolute, because of estimates, sampling and the limits of evidence.

Management prepares the financial statements. Management and those charged with governance are responsible for preventing and detecting fraud. The auditor must plan and perform the audit with professional scepticism, and must consider fraud under ISA 240. Revised versions of ISA 240 and ISA 570 apply to periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026.

International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) are issued by the IAASB. Firms also need quality management under ISQM 1.

sections.heading: Risk and materiality
sections.text:
Audit risk is the risk of giving an inappropriate opinion when the statements are materially misstated. It has three parts: inherent risk, control risk and detection risk. The auditor assesses the first two, and sets the amount of testing to bring detection risk to the level needed. ISA 315 (Revised 2019) requires this risk assessment, based on understanding the entity and its environment.

A misstatement is material if it could reasonably be expected to influence users’ decisions. ISA 320 mentions percentage benchmarks as a starting point, and the percentage is a matter of judgement.

Example: profit before tax is ₦50,000,000. The auditor uses 5% as a benchmark.
Materiality = 50,000,000 × 5% = ₦2,500,000.
At an illustrative 75%, performance materiality = ₦1,875,000.
Performance materiality is set lower to allow for undetected errors.

sections.heading: Internal control
sections.text: Internal control has five components under ISA 315: the control environment, the risk assessment process, monitoring, the information system and communication, and control activities. Strong controls may let the auditor rely on tests of control and reduce other testing. Significant deficiencies must be reported in writing to those charged with governance (ISA 265).

keyPoints: An audit gives reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance.
Management and those charged with governance are responsible for preventing fraud.
Audit risk has inherent, control and detection parts.
Materiality depends on influence on users’ decisions.
Revised ISA 240 and ISA 570 apply from periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026.

en.title: Auditing: evidence and reports
en.short: Types of audit evidence, sampling, going concern, and the audit opinions an auditor may give.

sections.heading: Gathering evidence
sections.text:
Under ISA 500, evidence must be sufficient, which concerns quantity, and appropriate, which concerns relevance and reliability. External evidence is generally more reliable than internal evidence.

Procedures include inspection, observation, external confirmation, recalculation, reperformance, analytical procedures and inquiry. Tests of controls check whether controls work. Substantive procedures look for misstatements in amounts and disclosures.

Assertions are the claims in the statements. They include existence, completeness, accuracy, valuation, rights and obligations, and cut-off. The test must match the assertion. To test receivables for existence, the auditor might ask customers to confirm their balances (ISA 505). To test the completeness of payables, the auditor would start from suppliers’ statements or later payments.

ISA 530 covers sampling. The sample must allow a reasonable basis for a conclusion on the whole population.

sections.heading: Going concern
sections.text: ISA 570 requires the auditor to evaluate management’s assessment of the entity’s ability to continue as a going concern. Warning signs include net liabilities, loan defaults and the loss of a major customer. The statements may still be properly prepared if a material uncertainty is adequately disclosed. The auditor then reports a separate section on it.

sections.heading: The audit report
sections.text:
ISA 700 covers the unmodified opinion and the form of report. For listed entities (publicly traded entities for periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026), ISA 701 requires key audit matters to be described. ISA 705 sets out modified opinions:

Material misstatement, material but not pervasive: qualified opinion (except for).
Material misstatement, material and pervasive: adverse opinion.
Unable to get enough evidence, material but not pervasive: qualified opinion.
Unable to get enough evidence, material and pervasive: disclaimer of opinion.

An emphasis of matter paragraph (ISA 706) draws attention to an item properly presented in the statements. It does not change the opinion.

Example: a Tanzanian trader’s inventory count was not attended, and the auditor has no other evidence. Inventory is material, but it does not affect most of the statements. The auditor gives a qualified opinion because of that limitation.

keyPoints: Evidence must be sufficient and appropriate.
Match each audit test to the assertion.
Test payables for completeness from outside sources.
An adverse opinion concerns a pervasive material misstatement.
A disclaimer concerns a pervasive lack of evidence.
Emphasis of matter does not modify the opinion.

en.title: Professional ethics for accountants
en.short: The IESBA Code’s principles, threats and safeguards, and how to work through a dilemma.

sections.heading: Fundamental principles
sections.text:
The International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA) issues a Code of Ethics. Many professional bodies base their rules on it. It sets out five fundamental principles:

Integrity: being straightforward and honest.
Objectivity: not allowing bias, conflict of interest or undue influence to override judgement.
Professional competence and due care: keeping skills up to date and working diligently.
Confidentiality: not disclosing information without proper authority, unless there is a legal or professional right or duty to do so.
Professional behaviour: complying with laws and avoiding conduct that discredits the profession.

sections.heading: Threats and safeguards
sections.text:
The Code uses a conceptual framework. The accountant must identify threats to the principles, evaluate them, and address them. There are five categories of threat:

Self-interest: a financial or other interest might influence judgement.
Self-review: relying on one’s own earlier work.
Advocacy: promoting a client’s position so far that objectivity suffers.
Familiarity: a long or close relationship makes one too sympathetic.
Intimidation: actual or perceived pressure deters objective action.

Safeguards reduce a threat to an acceptable level, such as review by another partner. If no safeguard works, the accountant should end or decline the engagement.

For auditors, independence is required in both mind and appearance. Holding a client’s shares would create a clear self-interest threat.

sections.heading: Working through a dilemma
sections.text:
A useful approach is to gather the facts, identify the principles at risk and the threats, consider the options, take advice if needed, document what was done and act.

Example: Esi is a financial controller in Accra. Her finance director tells her to record January sales in December, so that a bonus target is met. This threatens her integrity and creates intimidation. She can explain the accounting rule, keep records, and take the issue to the audit committee or a suitable senior person.

The Code also has provisions on non-compliance with laws and regulations (NOCLAR). Duties to report vary by country, so the local law must be checked.

keyPoints: The five principles are integrity, objectivity, competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour.
The five threats are self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation.
Identify threats, evaluate them and address them.
Auditors need independence of mind and in appearance.
Reporting duties under NOCLAR depend on local law.

en.title: Income tax computation
en.short: Worked personal and company tax for Nigeria under the 2025 Act, and rates in other countries.

sections.heading: Nigeria since 2026
sections.text:
Nigeria’s tax law changed greatly in 2025. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 took effect on 1 January 2026. It replaced older Acts, including the Companies Income Tax Act and Personal Income Tax Act. Companion Acts cover administration, the Nigeria Revenue Service and the Joint Revenue Board. Older books use old rates.

Companies pay 30% on taxable profit, with a 0% rate for small companies. A 4% development levy applies to assessable profits, before capital allowances, except for small and non-resident companies. Company capital gains are taxed at the company rate.

Two published texts of the Act differ, so check the current position with the Nigeria Revenue Service. Both set a small company’s fixed asset limit at ₦250 million.
The copy circulated from 2025, which state tax authorities publish: small company turnover up to ₦50 million, with professional services excluded. The 15% minimum effective tax rate covers members of multinational groups and other companies with turnover of ₦20 billion or more.
The copy released by the National Assembly in January 2026: turnover up to ₦100 million, with no such exclusion in the definition. The 15% rate covers members of groups with turnover of at least €750 million and other companies with turnover of ₦50 billion or more.

sections.heading: Worked examples for Nigeria
sections.text:
Personal tax bands (annual): first ₦800,000 at 0%; next ₦2,200,000 at 15%; next ₦9,000,000 at 18%; next ₦13,000,000 at 21%; next ₦25,000,000 at 23%; above ₦50,000,000 at 25%.

Adaeze earns ₦5,300,000 and pays rent of ₦1,500,000. Rent relief is 20% of rent, up to ₦500,000, so it is ₦300,000. Other deductions are ignored here.
Chargeable income = 5,300,000 − 300,000 = ₦5,000,000.
Tax = (2,200,000 × 15%) + (2,000,000 × 18%) = 330,000 + 360,000 = ₦690,000.

A large company has accounting profit of ₦80m, after depreciation of ₦12m and a disallowed fine of ₦1m. Capital allowances are ₦15m.
Assessable profit = 80 + 12 + 1 = ₦93m.
Taxable profit = 93 − 15 = ₦78m.
Tax at 30% = ₦23.4m.
Development levy at 4% of ₦93m = ₦3.72m.

sections.heading: Other countries
sections.text: At the time of writing, main company rates include 25% in Ghana, 30% in Kenya and 27% in South Africa. In the UK, the main rate is 25%, and a 19% small profits rate applies to profits under £50,000. Marginal relief applies between £50,000 and £250,000. Check the current official source.

keyPoints: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 took effect on 1 January 2026.
Nigeria’s general company rate is 30%, plus a 4% development levy on assessable profits.
Nigeria’s personal tax bands run from 0% to 25%.
Depreciation is added back, and capital allowances are deducted.
Rates differ by country, so name the country and check the year.

en.title: Corporate finance: investment appraisal
en.short: Time value of money, payback, NPV and IRR, with a worked capital project.

sections.heading: Time value of money
sections.text:
Corporate finance asks where a company should invest and how to pay for it.

Money today is worth more than the same sum later, because it can be invested and because of risk and inflation. Discounting converts a future amount to its present value:

PV = cash flow ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ

Here r is the required rate and n is the number of years.

sections.heading: The main methods
sections.text:
Payback is the time needed to recover the investment. It is simple, but it ignores later cash flows and the time value of money.

Net present value (NPV) is the sum of the present values of all cash flows. Accept a project if NPV is positive, because it earns more than the required return.

Internal rate of return (IRR) is the rate at which NPV is zero. Accept if IRR is above the required rate. IRR can mislead when projects are mutually exclusive, or when cash flows change sign more than once. In those cases, NPV is the better guide.

Use relevant cash flows only. Exclude depreciation, sunk costs and allocated overheads that do not change. Interest is also excluded, because the discount rate already covers the cost of finance. Include tax and working capital changes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A Ghanaian firm considers a project costing GH₵1,000,000. It gives net cash inflows of GH₵450,000 at the end of each of three years. The required return is 10%.

Payback = 1,000,000 ÷ 450,000 = 2.22 years.

Three-year annuity factor at 10% = 2.48685.
Present value of inflows is about GH₵1,119,083.
NPV is about GH₵119,083, which is positive.

At 20%, the annuity factor is 2.1065, so NPV is about −GH₵52,083.

Estimated IRR = 10% + 10% × 119,083 ÷ (119,083 + 52,083) = about 17.0%.
The exact IRR is about 16.6%. Interpolation gives a close estimate, not the exact figure.

keyPoints: Discounting converts future cash flows to present value.
Accept a project with a positive NPV, other things being equal.
IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero.
Exclude depreciation, sunk costs and interest from project cash flows.
NPV is the better guide when IRR conflicts with it.

en.title: Corporate finance: cost of capital and financing
en.short: CAPM, WACC, capital structure, dividend valuation and the management of working capital.

sections.heading: Sources of finance and cost of capital
sections.text:
Companies raise money through retained earnings, shares, loans, bonds, overdrafts and trade credit. Debt is usually cheaper than equity. Lenders face less risk, and interest is usually tax-deductible. However, debt increases financial risk.

The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) estimates the cost of equity:
Ke = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)

Rf is the risk-free rate, Rm is the market return, and beta (β) measures systematic risk.

Worked example in naira terms: Rf = 10%, Rm = 15%, β = 1.2.
Ke = 10% + 1.2 × 5% = 16%.
Pre-tax cost of debt = 12%, and tax rate = 30%.
After-tax Kd = 12% × (1 − 0.30) = 8.4%.
With 60% equity and 40% debt, at market values:
WACC = (0.60 × 16%) + (0.40 × 8.4%) = 9.6% + 3.36% = 12.96%.

The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) can be used as a discount rate for projects with similar risk to the existing business.

sections.heading: Capital structure and valuation
sections.text:
Modigliani and Miller argued in 1958 that, in a perfect market without taxes, capital structure does not change a firm’s value. Their later work added corporate tax, which gives debt a tax advantage. In practice, financial distress costs limit debt.

The dividend valuation model values a share from its expected dividends:
P₀ = D₁ ÷ (Ke − g)

Example: last year’s dividend is ₦2.00, expected growth (g) is 5%, and Ke is 15%.
D₁ = 2.00 × 1.05 = ₦2.10.
P₀ = 2.10 ÷ (0.15 − 0.05) = ₦21.

sections.heading: Working capital
sections.text:
Working capital is current assets less current liabilities. Too little causes liquidity problems. Too much ties up money.

Cash operating cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.

Example: 60 + 45 − 30 = 75 days. The firm must finance 75 days of its operations. It can shorten this by collecting faster. Delaying suppliers too long may cost discounts and their trust.

keyPoints: CAPM gives Ke as Rf plus beta times the market premium.
Use the after-tax cost of debt in WACC.
WACC suits projects with similar risk to the existing business.
Debt brings a tax benefit and also financial distress risk.
The cash cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days.

en.title: Public sector accounting
en.short: Government funds, budgets, cash and accrual accounting, IPSAS and public accountability.

sections.heading: Purpose and legal framework
sections.text:
Governments spend public money to deliver services, so accountability to the public and to parliament is central. Spending normally needs approval by the legislature through an appropriation.

In Nigeria, the 1999 Constitution creates the Consolidated Revenue Fund (section 80) and provides for the Auditor-General (section 85). Other important laws include the Finance (Control and Management) Act 1958, the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2007 and the Public Procurement Act 2007. Reform has been proposed, so check for changes. In Ghana, the main statute is the Public Financial Management Act 2016 (Act 921).

Independent audit and review by a public accounts committee complete the chain of accountability.

sections.heading: Standards and bases
sections.text:
The International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (IPSASB) issues IPSAS. It offers an accrual set of standards and a separate cash basis standard. Under the cash basis, only receipts and payments are recorded. It is simple and supports budget control, but it hides unpaid bills and the value of assets. The accrual basis records revenue and expenses when they arise, and shows assets and liabilities. It gives a fuller picture of the cost of services, but it requires better systems and skills.

Many countries, including Nigeria and Ghana, have moved toward accrual IPSAS, and progress varies between levels of government.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A Nigerian ministry receives an appropriation of ₦500m. Payments during the year are ₦420m, including a ₦60m vehicle with a five-year life. Unpaid invoices for services at the year end are ₦30m.

Cash basis expenditure = ₦420m.
Unspent appropriation = 500 − 420 = ₦80m.

Accrual basis expense:
Payments, excluding the vehicle: 420 − 60 = ₦360m.
Add unpaid invoices: ₦30m.
Add depreciation: 60 ÷ 5 = ₦12m.
Total = 360 + 30 + 12 = ₦402m.

The cash figure does not reveal the ₦30m owed or the vehicle held. Value for money audits ask a further question. Did the ministry use the money with economy, efficiency and effectiveness?

keyPoints: Public sector accounts focus on accountability, not profit.
Spending normally needs legislative appropriation.
IPSAS has an accrual set and a separate cash basis standard.
The accrual basis shows assets and unpaid liabilities.
Value for money means economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

en.title: Company law: directors, capital and auditors’ liability
en.short: Directors’ duties, share capital rules, dividends, minority protection and auditors’ liability.

sections.heading: Directors and members
sections.text:
Directors manage the company and owe duties to it, not usually to individual members. These duties include acting in good faith, for proper purposes, with care and skill, and avoiding conflicts of interest. CAMA 2020 in Nigeria, Act 992 in Ghana and the Companies Act 2006 in the UK each state such duties in their own terms.

Members make key decisions at general meetings. The UK case Foss v Harbottle (1843) says that the company itself is usually the proper claimant for a wrong done to it. Statutes and later cases give minority shareholders ways to bring a claim in some situations.

sections.heading: Capital and dividends
sections.text:
Share capital protects creditors, since it is a fund they rely on. So there are limits on returning it to members. Share premium and similar reserves are generally not available for dividends.

Dividends may be paid only out of distributable profits. In the UK these are accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses. Other countries have similar tests with their own details.

Example: Amina’s company has retained realised profits of ₦800,000 and a revaluation surplus of ₦500,000. The surplus is unrealised, so on this basis the maximum dividend is ₦800,000, not ₦1,300,000.

sections.heading: Auditors and insolvency
sections.text:
Company law sets out the auditor’s appointment, rights and removal. The auditor must use reasonable care and skill. The UK case Re Kingston Cotton Mill (1896) described the auditor as a watchdog, not a bloodhound, although modern standards expect more.

In Caparo Industries plc v Dickman (1990), the UK House of Lords held that auditors of a public company generally owed no duty of care to individual investors or potential investors who relied on the accounts. Courts in each country decide for themselves.

When a company cannot pay its debts, insolvency law applies. Options can include rescue, receivership and liquidation. CAMA 2020 added business rescue procedures, such as company voluntary arrangements and administration.

keyPoints: Directors owe their duties mainly to the company.
Foss v Harbottle makes the company the usual claimant.
Dividends may be paid only from distributable profits.
An unrealised revaluation surplus is generally not distributable.
Caparo limits auditors’ duty to individual investors in UK law.

en.title: Advanced financial reporting
en.short: Foreign operations, fair value, share-based payment and sustainability disclosure.

sections.heading: Foreign operations
sections.text:
IAS 21 asks each entity to identify its functional currency, which is the currency of its main economic environment. To consolidate a foreign subsidiary, the group translates its results into the presentation currency. Assets and liabilities use the closing rate. Income and expenses use the rates at transaction dates, or an average as an approximation. The exchange difference goes to OCI and is held in equity until disposal.

Example: a subsidiary’s opening net assets are $100,000, translated at ₦1,000 per dollar. Its profit is $20,000 at an average rate of ₦1,200. The closing rate is ₦1,500, and there are no dividends. Closing net assets are $120,000.

Opening net assets: 100,000 × 1,000 = ₦100m.
Profit: 20,000 × 1,200 = ₦24m.
Closing net assets: 120,000 × 1,500 = ₦180m.
Exchange gain in OCI = 180 − 100 − 24 = ₦56m.
Check: (100,000 × 500) + (20,000 × 300) = 50m + 6m = ₦56m.

In a hyperinflationary economy, IAS 29 also applies.

sections.heading: Measurement and judgement
sections.text:
IFRS 13 defines fair value as the price in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. It is an exit price. Its hierarchy ranks inputs. Level 1 uses quoted prices in active markets for identical items. Level 2 uses other observable inputs. Level 3 uses unobservable inputs. Level 3 needs the most judgement.

IFRS 2 covers share-based payment. For equity-settled awards to employees, an expense is measured at grant-date fair value and spread over the vesting period.

Advanced study also asks how standards affect behaviour, such as earnings management.

sections.heading: Sustainability reporting
sections.text: The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB), part of the IFRS Foundation, issued IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 in 2023. IFRS S1 sets general requirements for disclosing sustainability-related financial information. IFRS S2 covers climate. Each country decides whether and when to require them, so check your own regulator’s position.

keyPoints: Translate a foreign subsidiary’s assets and liabilities at the closing rate.
Translation differences on a foreign operation go to OCI.
IFRS 13 fair value is an exit price with a three-level hierarchy.
Equity-settled share awards use grant-date fair value.
IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 were issued by the ISSB in 2023.

en.title: Forensic accounting and fraud
en.short: Types of fraud, the fraud triangle, investigative techniques, evidence and famous failures.

sections.heading: What forensic accountants do
sections.text:
Forensic accounting applies accounting and investigative skills to legal questions. Work includes fraud investigations, tracing assets and giving expert evidence. An audit expresses an opinion on financial statements as a whole. An investigation focuses on a specific suspicion.

Fraud is often grouped as asset misappropriation, corruption and financial statement fraud. The fraud triangle, which builds on Donald Cressey’s research, explains why people commit it: pressure, opportunity and rationalisation.

Enron in the US used complex entities to hide debt and collapsed in 2001. Its failure helped bring about the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. Wirecard in Germany collapsed in 2020, after about €1.9 billion said to be held in trust accounts could not be found.

sections.heading: Techniques
sections.text:
Analytical tests look for what is unusual. Examples include duplicate payments, round amounts, payments just below approval limits, and bank accounts shared by employees and suppliers. Benford’s law predicts that in many natural data sets about 30.1% of numbers begin with the digit 1. A large departure raises a question, but it does not prove fraud.

Comparing payroll with staff records can reveal ghost employees.

The net worth method estimates hidden income. Example: an official’s net worth rises from ₦10m to ₦25m during a year. Known spending is ₦3m, and known legal income is ₦6m.
Unexplained funds = (25 − 10) + 3 − 6 = ₦12m.
This does not prove a crime, and the person may have an explanation, such as a gift or an inheritance.

sections.heading: Evidence and law
sections.text:
Evidence may reach a court, so it must be properly handled. A chain of custody records who held each item, and when. An expert witness owes a duty to help the court and must stay objective.

Anti-money laundering laws differ by country. Examples are Nigeria’s Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022, Ghana’s Anti-Money Laundering Act 2020 (Act 1044) and the UK’s Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. Check the current duties.

keyPoints: An investigation targets a specific suspicion, unlike a general audit.
The fraud triangle has pressure, opportunity and rationalisation.
Fraud is often grouped into misappropriation, corruption and statement fraud.
Benford’s law raises questions, and it does not prove fraud.
Chain of custody protects the value of evidence.

en.title: Research methods in accounting
en.short: Theories, research designs, data and statistics for an accounting dissertation.

sections.heading: Theory and questions
sections.text:
Research begins with a clear question that matters and can be answered. A literature review shows what is known and where a gap lies. Theory then explains why a relationship should exist.

Common theories include agency theory (Jensen and Meckling, 1976), which studies conflicts between owners and managers, and positive accounting theory (Watts and Zimmerman), which seeks to explain and predict the choices managers make. Ball and Brown’s 1968 study was an early example of research linking accounting earnings to share prices.

sections.heading: Choosing a design
sections.text:
Quantitative research tests hypotheses with numerical data. Archival studies use published accounts and market data, and event studies measure share price reactions to news. Surveys collect views from many people.

Qualitative research seeks depth and meaning through interviews, case studies and analysis of documents. It suits questions about how and why practices develop. Mixed methods combine the two.

Choose the design that fits the question. Consider access to data, and surveys’ risk of low response and bias.

Reliability means results are consistent. Validity means the study measures what it claims to measure. Generalisability is whether findings apply beyond the sample.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text:
Regression is widely used to study how a dependent variable relates to several others. It shows association. It does not show causation, because of omitted variables and reverse causality.

Example: a study regresses audit fees on company size and finds a coefficient of 0.60 on size, with a standard error of 0.20.
t = 0.60 ÷ 0.20 = 3.0.
At the usual 5% level, with a large sample, this is statistically significant. But statistical significance is not the same as economic importance.

Ethics applies at every stage. Obtain informed consent, protect the identity of participants and any confidential data, report results honestly and cite sources properly. Follow your institution’s rules on ethical approval, referencing and the use of AI tools.

keyPoints: A good study starts with a clear question and a gap in the literature.
Theory explains why a relationship should exist.
Choose the design to fit the question.
Regression shows association, not automatically causation.
Statistical significance is not the same as economic importance.
